metadata.file_name: International Labour Review - 2020 - AGASISTI - Tasks  occupations and wages in OECD countries.pdf
metadata.title: Tasks, occupations and wages in OECD countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses microdata from the 2011–12 PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills covering 21 OECD member countries (excluding Cyprus, the Russian Federation, and Australia for specific data-availability reasons). The authors apply final sampling weights in all regressions and compute jackknife replicate standard errors to account for the complex survey design. For the literacy cognitive score, they incorporate uncertainty by using the full set of plausible values for the PIAAC literacy assessment. In addition, the analytic sample is cleaned to ensure at least five observations in each country–occupation cell before estimating task-intensity indices and running pooled and country-specific models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explicitly reports plausible-value handling for the PIAAC literacy score (using REPEST in Stata and the full set of plausible values), but it does not describe any missing-data strategy for other variables (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation, or exclusion rules). Because the analysis relies on weighted regressions with replicate standard errors, the missing-data approach is likely embedded in the restricted scientific-use dataset preparation, but the authors do not document it. This is a reporting gap for transparency about how missing covariates were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the restricted PIAAC 2011–12 scientific-use dataset for 21 OECD member countries, excluding Cyprus and the Russian Federation (not OECD; and missing Moscow region for Russia) and excluding Australia because 3-digit occupational information is not available. For the 3-digit ISCO-08 occupation analysis, the dataset is cleaned to ensure at least five observations in each country–occupation cell; the pooled sample then contains 113 distinct occupational categories. All regressions are estimated on the resulting analytic sample and are weighted by final sampling weights; jackknife replicate standard errors are used throughout.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–12 (adult skills), pooled 21 OECD countries — literacy-based task intensity indices (abstract, routine, manual)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted pooled regressions with country fixed effects; R² (occupation FE vs no occupation FE): Abstract tasks 0.226→0.349, Routine tasks 0.050→0.077, Manual tasks 0.216→0.384. Literacy and education coefficients are statistically significant in pooled models; occupation fixed effects reduce coefficient magnitudes but keep them significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–12 data from 21 OECD countries, the study leveraged PIAAC literacy proficiency and educational attainment (plus demographic controls such as sex and immigrant status) to predict task intensity for abstract, routine, and manual tasks, finding that higher skills and education are positively associated with abstract and routine task performance and negatively associated with manual task performance. This indicates that adult skills and education are strongly linked to how workers are allocated to higher- and lower-demand task bundles, suggesting that upskilling and education policies may influence the task composition of jobs even after accounting for occupation structure.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–12 (adult skills), pooled 21 OECD countries — wage regressions (Mincerian wage equation augmented with task indices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: R² by specification (Table 3): (1) human capital only 0.432; (2) tasks only 0.318; (3) occupation dummies only 0.320; (4) human capital + tasks 0.473; (5) full model + occupation dummies 0.542. Effect sizes: 1 SD increase in abstract task index associated with ~7% higher hourly wage; manual tasks associated with ~5% wage penalty; routine tasks not significant after controlling for human capital.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–12 data from 21 OECD countries, the study leveraged PIAAC literacy proficiency, educational attainment, and job tenure together with abstract/routine/manual task indices to predict log hourly wages, finding that abstract tasks have a positive wage premium while manual tasks carry a wage penalty and routine tasks are near zero after controls. This indicates that labour-market returns align with task content (non-routine cognitive/abstract work rewarded, manual work penalized), supporting policy efforts that promote adult skill development and job matching toward higher-value task activities, while recognizing the authors’ explicit limitation that the estimates are descriptive rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–12 (adult skills), pooled 21 OECD countries — cross-country institutional factors for returns to abstract tasks
main_findings.target_variable: Country-level return to abstract tasks (coefficient from task–wage model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cross-country regression (Table 4): Gini coefficient 0.275 (SE 0.015, p<0.001); collective bargaining coverage (collbar) coefficient −0.001 (SE 0.000, p<0.001); R²=0.729.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–12 data from 21 OECD countries, the study leveraged country-level income inequality and collective bargaining coverage to explain variation in the estimated return to abstract tasks, finding that returns are higher where income inequality is wider and lower where unionization/collective bargaining coverage is stronger. This indicates that wage-task linkages are shaped by institutional context, suggesting that labour-market institutions and inequality-reduction strategies may moderate how strongly abstract task performance translates into earnings.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–12 (adult skills), pooled 21 OECD countries — within-occupation co-variation of task returns (Autor & Handel replication)
main_findings.target_variable: Co-variation of task returns within occupations (bivariate regressions of coefficients)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 5 (pooled sample): negative signs for intercept-related coefficients across bivariate relationships; N=113 occupations; R² values reported for each bivariate regression (e.g., 0.211, 0.347, 0.019, 0.326, 0.466, 0.447).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–12 data from 21 OECD countries, the study leveraged the estimated task-intensity effects within occupations to test within-occupation co-variation of returns, finding that the intercept-related coefficients are negative across the tested task-return pairings. This indicates that occupations with positive employment exhibit the predicted trade-off structure in task rewards, supporting the Autor–Handel task framework and implying that task-based wage inequality mechanisms are consistent across countries.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–12 (adult skills), pooled 21 OECD countries — self-selection into occupations (interaction model)
main_findings.target_variable: Self-selection into occupations along task dimensions (interaction terms in wage regressions)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 6 (pooled sample): interaction terms are strongly significant in specifications without and with individual-level controls; R² ranges from 0.392 to 0.484 across columns; N=65,217. Positive interaction terms indicate self-selection consistent with the theoretical predictions.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–12 data from 21 OECD countries, the study leveraged individual task intensity and occupation-level mean task intensity (plus individual controls such as gender, immigrant status, and quadratic polynomials in age and tenure) to predict log hourly wages, finding that the interaction terms are positive and statistically significant, consistent with workers self-selecting into occupations that reward the tasks they are relatively better at. This indicates that adult skill heterogeneity translates into occupational sorting along task dimensions, implying that policies affecting adult learning and skill acquisition can influence labour-market matching and wage outcomes through selection mechanisms.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses the 2011–12 PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills microdata for 21 OECD countries to examine how job task content relates to education, skills, occupational allocation, and wages. The authors construct standardized indices of abstract, routine, and manual task intensity from Likert-type task questions and estimate weighted pooled regressions with country fixed effects, occupation fixed effects (3-digit ISCO-08), and jackknife replicate standard errors. They incorporate PIAAC literacy uncertainty using the full set of plausible values via the REPEST Stata routine. In pooled models, R² rises from 0.226 to 0.349 for abstract tasks and from 0.216 to 0.384 for manual tasks when occupation dummies are added, while routine tasks remain low (≤0.077). In wage regressions, abstract tasks show a positive premium (~7% per 1 SD), manual tasks a penalty (~5%), and routine tasks are near zero after controls; cross-country institutional factors further explain variation in abstract-task returns. The paper is descriptive rather than causal, and it does not document a missing-data strategy beyond PV handling.
